# Diagnosing Sequential Misfires on the 2007 Dodge Caravan 3.3L

A misfire affecting cylinders 3 and 6 simultaneously on a 2007 Dodge Caravan with the 3.3L engine is not a random failure; it points directly to a shared resource or a specific control module issue. You have already eliminated the most common culprits by replacing spark plugs, ignition wires, the primary ignition coils, and the crankshaft position sensor. The fact that cylinders 1, 2, 4, and 5 are firing strongly while 3 and 6 show no spark confirms the problem is isolated to the upper intake manifold region or the engine control logic managing those specific outputs.

The physical layout of the 3.3L V6 engine places coils for cylinders 3 and 6 directly adjacent to each other on the top of the intake manifold, often sharing a common ignition coil pack or harness runner depending on the specific trim level and year revision. Since you have replaced the coils twice without success, we must shift focus from the components themselves to the power delivery path between the battery and the engine control unit (ECU).

When no spark reaches the plugs on two non-adjacent cylinders in a V6 configuration, the failure is frequently located at the high-voltage feed. Check the wiring harness that runs through the top of the intake manifold specifically where it enters the coil pack for cylinders 3 and 6. Even if visual inspection reveals no obvious cuts or burns, high-voltage electricity can arc internally within insulation layers or suffer from intermittent opens caused by vibration. Use a multimeter to verify continuity on the primary side of the ignition system leading to these specific coils while the engine is off. Look for high resistance in the wiring harness that often develops near mounting points where heat cycles cause plastic clips to crack over time.

Another critical component to investigate is the Engine Control Unit (ECU) itself, which you mentioned as a possibility. The ECU generates the initial trigger signal and manages the power distribution to the ignition coils. If the internal transistor or driver circuit responsible for firing cylinders 3 and 6 has failed internally, replacing the external coil packs will not resolve the issue because the control signal is never reaching the hardware. This scenario often presents exactly as described: strong spark on four cylinders and dead air on two specific ones after standard component replacement.

To isolate the ECU without a full swap, you can perform a cross-check if available. If you have access to a known good harness or coil pack set from another similar vehicle (like a Chrysler PT Cruiser or Grand Caravan), swapping the entire ignition harness assembly onto your engine will definitively rule out the wiring harness as the root cause. If the misfire persists with new external coils and verified good wires, the ECU is the likely suspect. This diagnosis requires careful consideration of cost versus repair time, as replacing a Powertrain Control Module (PCM) can be expensive if not covered by warranty or an extended coverage plan.

Before condemning the computer, ensure there are no blown fuses or damaged relays in the ignition control circuit. Some models utilize a relay dedicated to the secondary ignition system; a failing relay contacts could prevent power from reaching half of the coils while leaving the other half unaffected. Check the fuse box under the hood for any components labeled with "Ignition" or "Coil" functions that might have failed intermittently.

If all external wiring and power sources are confirmed good, and the ECU driver circuits are suspect, a professional scan tool capable of reading live ignition coil current data (if applicable to this specific platform) can sometimes reveal if the ECU is attempting to fire but failing due to an internal short, or if it has completely disabled the output. In many cases, these older Chrysler platforms have had documented issues with specific PCM revisions failing to drive certain cylinder banks correctly.

Addressing this requires methodical elimination. Since you have already replaced the primary suspect parts multiple times without resolution, the investigation must now move from mechanical components to electrical architecture and control logic. Patience in tracing the high-voltage path is essential, as visual inspection often misses internal wire degradation or controller board faults until a definitive electrical test confirms the open circuit location.
